lesson.title: Sum It Up: Detecting Errors with a Checksum
lesson.summary: A checksum protects a header and its data by adding all the bytes or words together with one's complement arithmetic, letting a receiver redo the same sum and confirm the result comes out to all 1 bits if nothing changed in transit.
lesson.body:
A single parity bit can only watch over a small group of bits at a time. Protecting an entire packet or an entire header with that same level of granularity would be expensive, so many protocols instead compute a checksum: a single value derived by arithmetically combining all the bytes, or larger chunks, in a message, then carried alongside the data so the receiver can redo the same arithmetic and confirm nothing changed.

The Internet checksum, used in the IPv4 header and in TCP and UDP headers, works by treating the data as a sequence of 16 bit words and adding them together using one's complement arithmetic, where any carry bit that overflows past the 16th bit gets wrapped around and added back into the bottom of the sum rather than discarded, a step called an end around carry. Once every word has been summed, the sender takes the one's complement, every bit flipped, of that final sum and places it in the checksum field of the header.

A small worked example makes the arithmetic concrete. Suppose there are just two 16 bit data words: 0xFFFF and 0x0001. Adding them in ordinary binary gives 0x10000, a 17 bit result. Under one's complement addition, that overflow bit is not discarded, it is carried around and added back to the remaining 16 bits, turning 0x10000 into 0x0001. The sender then flips every bit of 0x0001 to form the checksum, giving 0xFFFE, which travels in the header alongside the two original data words. When the receiver gets the message, it adds all three 16 bit values together, the two original data words plus the checksum field itself: 0xFFFF plus 0x0001 plus 0xFFFE, which works out to exactly 0xFFFF, a result of all 1 bits. That all ones result is the receiver's confirmation that nothing changed in transit, had even a single bit flipped somewhere in the header or data, the recomputed sum would almost certainly come out as something other than all 1s.

Because the checksum lives inside the packet's own header, alongside the data it protects, it travels with essentially no extra transmission overhead beyond the 16 bits the field itself occupies, one reason it remains standard across IP, TCP, and UDP decades after being designed. It is also comparatively cheap to compute compared to more sophisticated schemes, since it only requires simple addition rather than any division or lookup tables.

That cheapness comes with a real cost in detection power, though. Because addition is commutative, certain error patterns, such as two 16 bit words swapping places, or a matched increase in one word and decrease in another, leave the overall sum completely unchanged and pass through undetected. This gap is exactly what motivates the cyclic redundancy check, covered next, which replaces simple addition with a more structured operation specifically chosen to catch the error patterns a checksum tends to miss.
